questions.q: Why does {"name": "Ada", "role": "admin",} fail to parse as JSON?
options: Because "role" is not a valid key name
Because of the trailing comma after the last item, which JSON does not allow
Because JSON doesn't support string values
It actually parses fine
questions.explain: JSON strictly forbids a trailing comma after the final key/value pair or array item — one of the most common hand-written JSON errors.

questions.q: Why is {'name': 'Ada'} invalid JSON, even though it's valid Python/JavaScript?
options: JSON requires double quotes for strings and keys, not single quotes
JSON doesn't allow the key "name"
It's actually valid JSON
JSON requires no quotes at all
questions.explain: JSON strictly requires double quotes; single quotes are valid in Python/JS source code, which is exactly why this mistake is so easy to make when hand-writing JSON.

questions.q: Why can a very large integer ID silently lose precision when sent as a JSON number?
options: JSON numbers are always stored as text, so this can't happen
Many languages parse JSON numbers into a 64-bit float, which can't exactly represent integers past about 9 quadrillion
JSON has a hard limit of 100 for any number
This only happens with negative numbers
questions.explain: 64-bit floating point can't exactly represent every large integer, so very large IDs sent as JSON numbers can round — the fix is sending them as strings.

questions.q: What's the difference between {"nickname": null} and {} (nickname key absent entirely)?
options: There is no difference — both mean the exact same thing
null means the key exists with an explicitly empty value; an absent key means it was never sent at all
null is invalid JSON
An absent key always causes a parse error
questions.explain: null is an explicit value (the key exists, with 'nothing' as its value), while a missing key means the field wasn't included at all — a distinction that data.get() alone can hide.

questions.q: Why shouldn't code assume a documented 'string' field will always arrive as a string?
options: Because JSON doesn't actually support strings
Because an optional field documented as a string can still arrive as null when it has no value, and code assuming otherwise will crash
Because all fields are secretly numbers internally
Because field types never matter in practice
questions.explain: An optional field can be null even if its "normal" type is documented as string — handling only the common case leads to crashes on the optional one.
